title: Madho Das the ascetic
hookLine: at Nanded the Guru meets a Bairagi ascetic who becomes Banda, the servant

lines: NOBODY SITS ON THE MASTER'S COT.
cards: A hermitage by a river at Nanded, deep in the south. Its master is away. His disciples keep the place the way he likes it, and one thing above all: nobody sits on his cot.
Then a traveler arrives with his Sikhs, walks in, and sits down on it as if he lives there. Tradition says they try everything they know to tip the stranger off that cot, and nothing moves him.
Someone runs to fetch the master. The traveler is Guru Gobind Singh. The master hurrying home is an ascetic named Madho Das.

teach.h: A BAIRAGI WHO LET GO OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: Madho Das was a Bairagi, a renunciant, someone who had let go of attachment. He had left home and family behind, lived as a holy man, and gathered his own followers; tradition says people feared his powers.
Picture him arriving, out of breath, at his own door, and finding a man calmly sitting where no one may sit. Tellings vary, but the heart of it is a short exchange. Madho Das asks who this is.

teach.h: HE FINDS THE GURU ON HIS COT.
teach.b: The Guru answers, in effect, that it's someone Madho Das already knows. And something in him gives way.
He says he is the Guru's banda. The word means servant, even bondsman: not a title anyone would choose to look important. That's the turn the Sikh story cares about.

teach.h: CALLED BACK INTO THE WORLD TO SERVE.
teach.b: Here was a man who had already given up the world, and the Guru's call was not to give up more, but to come back into it: to carry a household's burdens, a people's troubles, and to serve.
In the Sikh telling, the hermit's discipline isn't thrown away. It gets a new direction. Tradition says he takes amrit and becomes Banda Singh, though tellings differ on the name he received.
Sikhs also remember him as Bahadur, the brave.
But the name that stuck first is the one he gave himself at the cot. The Khalsa's hard years begin with him, and some of them are difficult to hear. Notice that it doesn't begin with a battle.
It begins with one man deciding whom he serves.

how: Sikhs tell the meeting of Guru Gobind Singh and Madho Das at Nanded as the beginning of Banda Singh Bahadur's story, and remember that he first named himself the Guru's banda, his servant.

o: a Sufi friend who sheltered the Guru's sons
the hermit at Nanded who became Banda Singh
the Guru's scribe who wrote out the scripture

games.q: who's who at the hermitage — tap the pairs.
p: the seat nobody else could sit on
the brave, as Sikhs remember him

s: Madho Das was a soldier when he met the Guru
he was a Bairagi, a holy man who had left the world behind.
in the story, the Guru sits on the cot nobody was allowed to use
tradition says the disciples could not move him off it.
the name Banda was a grand title he was given
in the Sikh telling he called himself banda, the Guru's servant.

games.q: you come home to your hermitage and a stranger is sitting calmly on your cot, the one nobody touches. what do you do?
o: throw him out with everything you've got.
ask who he is, and listen.
leave and find somewhere else to live.
games.why: in the Sikh telling, Madho Das asks who he is, and by the end of the exchange calls himself the Guru's banda.

practice: Think of where you usually sit in your day: the seat nobody else takes, the routine nobody interrupts.
Now picture one person whose day would be lighter if you set that seat aside, and one plain task you could do for them, without being asked and without mentioning it afterward.
If you pray, you can repeat Waheguru on each breath out while you hold that picture.

wordCard.voice: Madho Das. The Bairagi holy man at Nanded who, in Sikh tradition, met Guru Gobind Singh, called himself the Guru's banda, and became Banda Singh.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: banda, servant; the name Madho Das gave himself before the Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: the servant. A hermit's discipline, given a new direction. Day eight hundred thirty-seven, done.
